extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or graduate students in mathematical logic / model theory
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook section covering (1) definitions and theorems about adding defined function symbols and interpretations between first-order theories, including syntactic translation and eliminability of definitions; and (2) construction and basic properties of nonstandard analysis (*R), finite/infinitesimal elements, standard part, and nonstandard characterizations of convergence and differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ∀2 validity decidability (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the set of valid ∀2 sentences is decidable. (A ∀2 formula is one of the form ∀ x1 · · · ∀ xm ∃ y1 · · · ∃ yn θ where θ is quantifier-free.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: this is a solvable subcase of the general decision problem of first-order logic, which is undecidable by Church's theorem. The exercise identifies a syntactic fragment (∀*∃* with quantifier-free matrix) whose validity set is decidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncreative definition equivalence (Theorem 27A)
rubrics_metrics.description:
(a) (The definition is noncreative.) For any sentence σ in the smaller language, if T; δ |= σ (in the augmented language), then already T |= σ.
(b) (f is well defined.) The sentence ∀ v1 ∃!v2 ϕ (ε) is in the theory T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two conditions are equivalent: a definition δ of a new function symbol f by ∀v1 ∀v2( f v1 = v2 ↔ ϕ ) is noncreative (adds no new consequences in the original language) iff T proves uniqueness-existence ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ. The proof constructs the interpretation A↦(A,F) when T proves ε, and conversely δ implies ε syntactically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good form for defining new function symbols (δ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of a one-place function symbol f by the sentence (δ): ∀ v1 ∀ v2[ f v1 = v2 ↔ ϕ], where ϕ is a formula in the original language in which only v1 and v2 may occur free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: A definition should designate unique objects (be well-defined). The textbook warns against 'definitions' that assign ambiguous values (example: f defined by f(v)=y iff v<y causing contradictions) and prescribes the form δ together with the requirement that T proves ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ to guarantee noncreativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an interpretation π of language L0 into theory T1
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation π of L0 into T1 is a function on the set of parameters of L0 such that: 1. π assigns to ∀ a formula π∀ of L1 in which at most v1 occurs free, and T1 |= ∃ v1 π∀. 2. π assigns to each n-place predicate parameter P a formula πP of L1 in which at most v1,…,vn occur free. 3. π assigns to each n-place function symbol f a formula πf of L1 in which at most v1,…,vn,v_{n+1} occur free, such that T1 |= ∀ v1 · · · ∀ vn(π∀(v1) → … → π∀(vn) → ∃ x(π∀(x) ∧ ∀ v_{n+1}(πf(v1,…,vn+1) ↔ v_{n+1} = x))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation data specify how to pick a 'universe' inside models of T1 (π∀) and how to interpret predicates and function symbols on that universe. Conditions ensure π∀ defines a nonempty domain and πf defines a unique output inside that domain for each tuple of domain elements. Constants are special cases (n=0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing πB and π^{-1}[T1]
rubrics_metrics.description: Given interpretation π and model B of T1, define |πB| as the set defined in B by π∀; P^{πB} as the relation defined by πP restricted to |πB|; f^{πB}(a1,…,an) = the unique b with |=B πf[[a1,…,an,b]]. Define π^{-1}[T1] = Th{πB | B ∈ Mod T1} = {σ | σ is an L0-sentence true in every structure πB obtainable from a model B of T1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: π^{-1}[T1] is a theory capturing all L0-sentences true in all π-extracted structures from models of T1. It is satisfiable iff T1 is satisfiable. This gives a semantic way to see what T1 'interprets' as L0-theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: definition as interpretation (identity except f)
rubrics_metrics.description: When augmenting T by a definition δ of f with π identity except πf = ϕ, if T proves ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ then π is an interpretation and π^{-1}[T] = Cn(T; δ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows that a proper definition of f corresponds to an interpretation of the extended language into the original theory; definitional extension is eliminable and gives no new consequences in the original language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm for syntactical translation ϕ ↦ ϕ^π
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ϕ^π by recursion: for atomic α with function symbols, scan α right-to-left; replace a rightmost function term g x1…xn by a fresh variable y and prefix ∀y(πg(x1,…,xn,y) → …); replace predicate P by πP. For connectives: (¬ϕ)^π = ¬(ϕ^π), (ϕ→ψ)^π = (ϕ^π → ψ^π), and quantifiers are relativized: (∀x ϕ)^π = ∀x(π∀(x) → ϕ^π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recursive translation effectively replaces terms by relations guaranteeing the functional graph, and relativizes quantifiers to the domain defined by π∀. The translation preserves truth via Lemma 27B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of syntactic translation (Lemma 27B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let π be an interpretation of L0 into T1 and B a model of T1. For any formula ϕ of L0 and any map s of variables into |πB|, |=_{πB} ϕ[s] iff |=_B ϕ^π [s].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma justifies that ϕ^π speaks 'the same thing' in B that ϕ speaks in the extracted structure πB; proof by induction on formula complexity and number of function-symbol places in atomic formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary on π^{-1}[T1] and translation (Corollary 27C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sentence σ of L0, σ ∈ π^{-1}[T1] iff σ^π ∈ T1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a tight connection between the semantic π^{-1} image and syntactic translation: sentences true in all πB (models extracted from T1 models) correspond exactly to those whose translations are consequences of T1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of theories and faithfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation π of a theory T0 into a theory T1 is an interpretation π of the languages such that T0 ⊆ π^{-1}[T1]. If T0 = π^{-1}[T1], π is a faithful interpretation (then σ ∈ T0 ⇔ σ^π ∈ T1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faithfulness means T1 exactly captures T0 under π-translation. This provides a formal notion of when one theory 'is as strong as' another even in different languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitional eliminability (Theorem 27D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given T containing ε = ∀ v1 ∃!v2 ϕ and δ = ∀ v1 ∀ v2( f v1 = v2 ↔ ϕ ), and π the identity on parameters except πf = ϕ, then for any L^+ sentence σ there is an original-language sentence σ^π such that (a) T; δ |= (σ ↔ σ^π). (b) T; δ |= σ ⇐⇒ T |= σ^π. (c) If f does not occur in σ, then |= (σ ↔ σ^π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes that proper definitional extensions are eliminable: every statement about the extended language is equivalent (over T;δ) to one in the original language. In particular, new defined symbols add convenience but no essential content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a nonstandard model *R (via compactness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a very large language with symbols for every relation and operation on R and constants c_r for each real r. Consider Th(R) ∪ { c_r < v1 | r ∈ R }. Any finite subset is satisfiable in R by choosing a large real for v1, so by compactness there is a structure A and element a with these sentences true; A ≡ R and contains an element a satisfying r < a for all standard r. From A obtain *R isomorphic to A with R as substructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction demonstrates existence of nonstandard extensions of R with infinite and infinitesimal elements. Key tools: expand language with names for all standard elements/relations, add infinitude axioms, apply compactness, then repair to get *R containing R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer principle method (expressible properties carry over)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property of relations or operations on R can be expressed by a sentence of the language, then that sentence holds in R and hence in *R (since *R ≡ R); thus ∗< is transitive, ∗+ is commutative, and field axioms hold in *R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard model-theoretic transfer: elementary (first-order) properties are preserved between elementarily equivalent structures. It justifies reasoning about *R by checking sentences in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of F (finite elements) and I (infinitesimals)
rubrics_metrics.description:
F = {x ∈ *R | ∗|x| ∗< y for some y ∈ R}.
I = {x ∈ *R | ∗|x| ∗< y for all positive y ∈ R}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These first-order-definable sets separate finite (bounded by some standard real) and infinitesimal (smaller than any positive standard real) elements of *R. Use them to study algebraic and topological properties in nonstandard analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic closure properties of F and I (Theorem 28A)
rubrics_metrics.description:
(a) F is closed under addition ∗+, subtraction ∗−, and multiplication ∗·.
(b) I is closed under addition ∗+, subtraction ∗−, and multiplication, and x ∈ I and z ∈ F ⇒ x ∗· z ∈ I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraically: F is a subring of *R and I is an ideal of F. These closure properties are proven by transferring standard inequalities and using bounds by standard reals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitely-close relation # and its properties (Definition & Theorem 28B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define x is infinitely close to y (written x # y) iff x ∗− y is infinitesimal. Theorem 28B: (a) # is an equivalence relation on *R. (b) If u # v and x # y, then u ∗+ x # v ∗+ y and ∗− u # ∗− v. (c) If u # v and x # y and x,y,u,v are finite, then u ∗· x # v ∗· y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures the natural algebraic compatibility of infinitesimal proximity: addition, negation, and (for finite elements) multiplication respect the equivalence classes of #. Use ideal properties of I in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of standard point between finitely-separated near elements (Lemma 28C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x # y and at least one is finite, then there is a standard q strictly between x and y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is used to deduce uniqueness of standard parts and related separation facts; the proof uses the finiteness of one element to find a standard positive bound and produce an intermediate standard q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard part existence and uniqueness (Theorem 28D & Corollary 28E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every x ∈ F is infinitely close to a unique r ∈ R. Corollary: Each finite x has a unique decomposition x = s ∗+ i where s is standard and i is infinitesimal; s is called st(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard part map st: F → R is well-defined and surjective; it identifies the unique standard real infinitely close to a finite nonstandard real. This provides a bridge back to standard analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of the standard-part map st (Theorem 28F)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) st maps F onto R. (b) st(x) = 0 iff x is infinitesimal. (c) st(x ∗+ y) = st(x) + st(y). (d) st(x ∗· y) = st(x) · st(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In algebraic terms, st is a ring homomorphism from F onto R with kernel I, so F/I ≅ R. These properties validate taking standard parts of sums/products of finite nonstandard numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard definition of convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F : R → R. Then F converges at a to b iff whenever x is infinitely close to (but different from) a, then ∗F(x) is infinitely close to b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is equivalent to the usual ε–δ definition: the equivalence follows by formalizing the ε–δ sentence and transferring to *R. The nonstandard formulation often simplifies reasoning: lim_{x→a} F(x) = st(∗F(a + i)) for any nonzero infinitesimal i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard characterization of continuity (Corollary 28G)
rubrics_metrics.description: F is continuous at a iff whenever x # a, then ∗F(x) # F(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity is encoded by preservation of infinitesimal proximity by the function's *-extension; this is a direct corollary of the nonstandard convergence definition with b = F(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard derivative definition and chain rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative: F'(a) = b iff for every nonzero infinitesimal dx we have dF/dx # b, where dF = ∗F(a+dx) − F(a). Chain rule: If G'(a) and F'(G(a)) exist then (F◦G)'(a) exists and equals F'(G(a)) · G'(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivatives are defined by infinitesimal quotients; the chain rule proof uses infinitesimal calculus algebraically via dF,dG and uses continuity and basic arithmetic of infinitesimals/finite elements. The nonstandard approach replaces ε–δ estimates with manipulations of infinitesimals.
